articles.title: Watch: BBC joins police on front line against car theft

articles.title: Watch: Hong Kong displays Van Gogh painting not seen publicly in 60 years
articles.summary: Châtaigniers en fleurs, also known as Chestnut Trees in Blossom, is expected to receive record bids at auction this weekend.
articles.body:
One of Vincent van Gogh's paintings not seen publicly for more than 60 years has drawn crowds in Hong Kong, where it has been displayed ahead of auction this weekend in New York.

Van Gogh painted Châtaigniers en fleurs (Chestnut Trees in Blossom) in the French village of Auvers-sur-Oise, about two months before he died in 1890.

Sotheby's estimates the painting will fetch $180m (£136m), which would mark the highest auction price for a Van Gogh artwork.

articles.title: Bengaluru police lodge FIR on KADA special officer Vikas Marmat following a late night raid on a Bar & Rest on Oct 10
articles.summary: BENGALURU: Cubbon Park police in Bengaluru have registered an FIR against Kuppam Area Development Authority special officer Vikas Marmat and three others
articles.body: BENGALURU: Cubbon Park police in Bengaluru have registered an FIR against Kuppam Area Development Authority special officer Vikas Marmat and three others following a citywide late-night crackdown on pubs, bars and restaurants on October 9-10.In his complaint leading to the FIR, police inspector Arun Salunke said that, acting on the orders of the Bengaluru city police commissioner, he and several other police officers had been tasked with checking for underage individuals and suspicious persons at pubs, bars and restaurants within the limits of Cubbon Park and Ashok Nagar police stations around midnight on October 9.When Salunke, along with police personnel identified as BS Ashoka, Balaram Nayak and others, reached Cavore Bar and Restaurant on Residency Road to check identity cards and verify the ages of those present, four individuals allegedly got into an argument with the complainant and other police personnel over trivial issues.They also allegedly verbally abused Salunke and the other officers present.The commotion and altercation were recorded, and videos of the incident went viral on social media platforms on Tuesday.Following Salunke’s complaint, Cubbon Park police registered a case against Marmat, Abhay Uday Singh, Nitish and Roshan under various sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), including Section 115(2) (voluntarily causing hurt), Section 351(2) (criminal intimidation), Section 352 (intentional insult with intent to provoke a breach of peace), Section 132 (assault or criminal force to deter a public servant from discharging their duty) and Section 133 (assault or criminal force with intent to dishonour a person).The 2019-batch IAS officer has been named as the prime accused, while the other three individuals have been articles.title: After 50 days atop 200-foot tower in Punjab, 2 elderly dam oustees climb down
articles.summary: PATHANKOT: After enduring 50 days of inclement weather on a makeshift tarpaulin platform atop a 200-foot-high electricity tower, two elderly men in their
articles.body: PATHANKOT: After enduring 50 days of inclement weather on a makeshift tarpaulin platform atop a 200-foot-high electricity tower, two elderly men in their seventies and eighties ended their protest and climbed down on Monday following an assurance from the district administration that a meeting with Punjab Water Resources Minister Barinder Kumar Goyal would be arranged within a week.The two protesters, Sharm Singh, 82, and Kulwinder Singh, 72, had climbed the tower on August 25 near the residence of the Pathankot deputy commissioner in Madhour village, around 10 km from the city, to press their demands concerning the Shahpur Kandi Dam project.Dayal Singh, president of the Barrage Oustees Sangharsh Committee, said the two men agreed to end their protest after the district administration assured them of a meeting with the minister and the secretary of the Water Resources Department.Speaking to TOI after returning home, Kulwinder Singh said the administration and the dam authorities had assured them that the meeting would take place within a week. “We have climbed down on the assurance that our grievances will be heard. If the government fails to address our demands, it should be prepared for a bigger agitation,” he said.The protesters are demanding the termination of around three dozen people appointed by the dam management or jobs for their kin. Kulwinder said their land had been acquired for the construction of the dam for a meagre compensation of Rs 2,700 per kanal. They were also promised jobs for their children, but their expectations remained unfulfilled, he alleged. He said their protest was aimed at securing justice for the oustees who had sacrificed their land for the project but were still waiting for the promised rehabilitation and employment opportunities.Asked how they managed to spend 50 days atop the tower, exposed to heavy rain, storms and other weather conditions, Kulwinder said the hardships had only strengthened their resolve. The two men remained on a makeshift platform measuring nearly 4 feet by 4 feet, braving the elements while their families and supporters waited anxiously for a resolution. The height and precarious conditions made their protest physically demanding, particularly given their advanced age.However, they remained determined to continue their struggle until their demands were addressed. Kulwinder said climbing down did not mean they had abandoned their cause. They had accepted the administration's assurance in the hope that the promised meeting would lead to a concrete decision. articles.standfirst: Vazão na estrutura chega a 11,4 milhões de litros de água por segundo. Calhas permanecem abertas para controlar o nível do reservatório após as fortes chuvas que atingiram a região.
articles.summary: Vazão na estrutura chega a 11,4 milhões de litros de água por segundo. Calhas permanecem abertas para controlar o nível do reservatório após as fortes chuvas que atingiram a região.
articles.body:
Vertedouro de Itaipu libera volume de água 7 vezes maior que vazão média das Cataratas — Foto: Itaipu Binacional

Com a abertura do vertedouro da Usina Hidrelétrica de Itaipu, em Foz do Iguaçu, no oeste do Paraná, a vazão chegou a 11,4 milhões de litros de água por segundo . O volume poderia encher cerca de 274 piscinas olímpicas com 2.500 m³ por minuto .

A quantidade de água é equivalente a sete vezes a vazão média das Cataratas do Iguaçu. Segundo a Itaipu Binacional, duas calhas permanecem abertas para controlar o nível do reservatório após as fortes chuvas que atingiram a região.

As dez comportas abertas ficam na calha esquerda e central do vertedouro. Ao todo, a estrutura possui três calhas e 14 comportas.

O vertedouro está aberto de forma ininterrupta desde 30 de setembro. A calha central foi aberta nesta terça-feira (13). Conforme a Itaipu, a operação deve continuar até que o volume de água que chega ao reservatório diminua e seja possível controlar o nível apenas por meio da geração de energia.

🔎 O que é um vertedouro e por que ele precisa ser aberto? O vertedouro funciona como uma espécie de "válvula de alívio" da usina, que permite liberar o excesso de água do reservatório . As comportas são abertas quando o volume de água que chega à usina é maior do que aquele que pode ser utilizado para gerar energia ou armazenado com segurança. A medida ajuda a controlar o nível do reservatório e evitar que a água ultrapasse os limites previstos para a operação da usina.

A abertura das comportas não afeta o fornecimento de eletricidade. A usina informou que continua atendendo normalmente à demanda de Brasil e Paraguai.

Vertedouro foi aberto outras vezes em 2026

Esta não é a primeira operação do vertedouro de Itaipu neste ano. A estrutura foi aberta entre 28 de junho e 5 de julho e voltou a operar em 12 de julho.

Em setembro, o vertedouro foi aberto novamente no dia 13. Desde então, houve aberturas e fechamentos conforme as condições dos rios e a necessidade de controlar o nível do reservatório.

Em 22 de setembro, por exemplo, o vertedouro foi fechado às 10h25. A estrutura voltou a operar posteriormente e permanece aberta sem interrupções desde 30 de setembro.

Por que Itaipu precisa abrir o vertedouro?

Calha esquerda do vertedouro está aberta desde o dia 30 — Foto: Itaipu Binacional

O vertedouro é uma estrutura utilizada para liberar o excesso de água do reservatório quando o volume que chega à usina supera a quantidade que pode ser utilizada para produzir energia.

Itaipu é uma hidrelétrica do tipo fio d'água, com capacidade relativamente limitada de armazenar grandes volumes adicionais de água.

Por isso, em períodos de chuvas intensas, a abertura das comportas ajuda a controlar o nível do reservatório e manter a operação da usina dentro dos limites de segurança.

A Itaipu informou que acompanha as condições dos rios e as previsões de chuva para definir quando será possível encerrar o vertimento.

articles.title: Morte de pesquisadora russa por peste gera preocupação global | G1
articles.standfirst: Relatos conflitantes sobre o que causou a morte de uma técnica de laboratório em um instituto russo de pesquisa sobre a peste estão gerando preocupação global. Veja aqui o que você precisa saber.
articles.summary: Com a morte de Darya Shipilova por suposta peste pneumônica na Rússia, microbiologista analisa os riscos de um surto e a falta de clareza nos dados oficiais.
articles.body:
A morte de uma pesquisadora russa especializada em peste explicada por um microbiologista — Foto: Adobe Stock

Informações contraditórias sobre a morte de uma funcionária de laboratório em um instituto russo de pesquisa sobre a peste estão alimentando temores quanto à possibilidade de propagação da peste pneumônica.

Quase 200 pessoas estão em quarentena na Sibéria depois que Darya Shipilova, de 28 anos, adoeceu no trabalho e faleceu posteriormente, em 2 de outubro.

As circunstâncias exatas de sua morte são desconhecidas. Uma alta autoridade russa publicou nas redes sociais na semana passada que Shipilova “havia morrido de peste” – antes de editar a postagem para acrescentar “possivelmente”. Desde então, o órgão regulador da saúde da Rússia declarou que ela morreu de “pneumonia de etiologia desconhecida”.

Reportagens da mídia local sugeriram que ela teria sido infectada após um acidente no laboratório onde trabalhava, o Instituto de Pesquisa Antipeste de Irkutsk da Sibéria e do Extremo Oriente. Mas essas informações não foram confirmadas.

Então, o que é a peste e como ela se espalha? Devemos nos preocupar?

O que é a peste? Existem diferentes tipos?

A peste é causada pela bactéria Yersinia pestis . A bactéria geralmente vive em roedores que habitam o solo, como ratos e cães-da-pradaria, mas também pode infectar seres humanos.

A mesma bactéria Y. pestis pode causar três tipos diferentes de peste.

A peste bubônica é transmitida de animais para humanos por pulgas e causa inchaço (chamado de bubões) nos gânglios linfáticos. Outros sintomas incluem febre, dor de cabeça, calafrios e fraqueza.

A peste bubônica pode matar em poucos dias se não forem usados antibióticos. Entre 30% e 60% das pessoas que contraem essa forma de peste morrerão.

A peste septicêmica ocorre se a peste bubônica não for tratada , ou pode ocorrer diretamente se a doença entrar na corrente sanguínea. A peste septicêmica causa sangramento nos órgãos e seu nome se refere à grave infecção sanguínea, a septicemia, que essa forma da doença pode causar.

A peste pneumônica – a causa suspeita, mas não confirmada, da morte de Shipilova na Sibéria – pode ocorrer quando a peste bubônica se espalha para os pulmões . Mas a peste pneumônica também pode se espalhar de pessoa para pessoa por meio de minúsculas gotículas respiratórias.

A peste pneumônica é a forma mais rara, mas a mais grave da peste. A taxa de mortalidade chega a 100% se não for tratada.

Além dos outros sintomas, a peste pneumônica inclui pneumonia grave – uma infecção nos pulmões, neste caso causada por bactérias.

A peste bubônica foi responsável pela morte de dezenas de milhões de pessoas no Mediterrâneo ocidental entre 541 e 750 d.C. (a chamada Peste de Justiniano) e depois matou até metade da população da Europa na Idade Média (agora chamada de “Peste Negra”).

Mas tem havido surtos da doença desde a época medieval.

Uma terceira pandemia, que se estendeu pelo final do século XIX e início do século XX, matou até 12 milhões de pessoas.

A peste ainda é endêmica na Ásia Central, na África, nas Américas e na Sibéria, onde a técnica de laboratório russa faleceu na semana passada. Isso significa que ela está presente em um nível estável e consistente nessas regiões.

Os casos geralmente ocorrem em áreas rurais e agrícolas, o que torna improvável um possível vazamento de laboratório em uma área urbana.

Sim. Um tratamento com antibióticos de 10 a 14 dias (por via oral ou intravenosa) trata a peste – desde que ele seja iniciado logo após a infecção.

Mas desde 1995 várias cepas da peste resistentes a antibióticos foram detectadas na natureza.

Na década de 1980, cientistas da União Soviética também criaram cepas resistentes – essa história serve de base para cenários hipotéticos envolvendo guerra biológica.

Não há evidências, porém, de que a cepa que supostamente teria matado Shipilova não pudesse ser tratada com antibióticos, ou de que o laboratório esteja pesquisando armas biológicas.

Houve apenas um grande surto documentado de peste pneumônica, na década de 1910, na China.

Ainda não sabemos muito sobre o caso na Sibéria. Mas, neste momento, há poucas evidências que justifiquem preocupação com a possibilidade de uma epidemia (que é localizada) ou de uma pandemia (que envolve vários países).

Em um comunicado divulgado na última segunda-feira, 5 de outubro, a Organização Mundial da Saúde ( OMS ) afirmou estar ciente de relatos de que uma funcionária de laboratório em Irkutsk teria “morrido de pneumonia grave”, mas que a causa da morte ainda não havia sido oficialmente confirmada.

O comunicado da OMS também afirmou: “Com base nas informações não oficiais disponíveis, o risco à saúde pública para a população em geral parece ser baixo. A avaliação de risco será atualizada assim que mais informações estiverem disponíveis”.

Para avaliar esse risco, será essencial ter acesso a informações transparentes sobre como Shipilova adoeceu e faleceu.

Thomas Jeffries é professor Sênior de Microbiologia da Western Sydney University. articles.title: Mortes de irmãs por falsos policiais teriam relação com facções | G1
articles.standfirst: Corpos das vítimas, de 15 e 17 anos, foram achados em uma área de mata, em Tauá, no interior do estado. Elas foram tiradas à força da casa onde moravam com os avós.
articles.summary: Corpos das vítimas, de 15 e 17 anos, foram achados em uma área de mata, em Tauá, no interior do estado. Elas foram tiradas à força da casa onde moravam com os avós.
articles.body:
As mortes das duas irmãs em Tauá , no interior do Ceará, estaria relacionada com o envolvimento das vítimas com uma facção criminosa e um relacionamento amoroso de uma delas . O g1 obteve, nesta terça-feira (13), informações sobre a investigação do duplo homicídio. Quatro criminosos, que fingiram ser policiais, são apontados como responsáveis pelo crime.

Os corpos das vítimas, que tinham 15 e 17 anos, foram encontrados com marcas de tiros , na manhã desta terça-feira, na comunidade de Angicos, em Tauá . Elas foram levadas à força da casa onde moravam com os avós, em Arneiroz , município vizinho. Um suspeito foi preso nesta terça-feira.

O g1 apurou, com fontes policiais, que as vítimas se mudaram para Arneiroz para tentar fugir de uma facção criminosa. As investigações apontam que elas teriam relação com o Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC), facção de origem paulista, em Tauá. A adolescente mais nova tinha passagem pela polícia por ato infracional análogo ao crime de furto.

Porém, uma delas teria começado um relacionamento amoroso com um homem que faz parte da facção rival , o Comando Vermelho (CV), organização criminosa de origem carioca também com atuação no Ceará. Os membros do PCC, então, passaram a desconfiar que as irmãs teriam "virado" para o CV, ou seja, passado de um grupo criminoso para o outro.

Irmãs levadas à força por criminosos em Arneiroz foram encontradas mortas em Tauá. — Foto: Flaviano Oliveira/ Arquivo pessoal

Nesta terça, Antônio Wellington Alves Pires, de 27 anos, foi preso apontado como suspeito de envolvimento no duplo homicídio. Ele foi capturado em Tauá, onde as irmãs foram achadas mortas.

Antônio Wellington responde por tráfico de drogas. Ele foi conduzido à Delegacia de Tauá, onde foi autuado em flagrante por homicídio qualificado, permanecendo à disposição da Justiça.

A Secretaria da Segurança Pública e Defesa Social do Ceará (SSPDS) disse que segue com as diligências em andamento com o objetivo de identificar e capturar outros suspeitos de envolvimento com o crime.

Suspeito de matar irmãs levadas à força de casa é preso no Ceará. — Foto: Reprodução

O g1 apurou com fontes policiais que quatro criminosos chegaram à casa das vítimas, na localidade de Cachoeira de Fora, utilizando um carro branco. Eles exigiram a presença das jovens e alegaram que eram policiais.

Os criminosos renderam as duas jovens e prenderam as mãos delas usando abraçadeiras de nylon. Antes de sair da residência, eles assumiram para a família das vítimas que não eram policiais e que iriam matar as duas adolescentes .

articles.title: Inteligência emocional: estudo com 600 mil pessoas revela diferenças | G1
articles.standfirst: Nova pesquisa é um dos maiores estudos sobre inteligência emocional realizados até o momento, abrangendo dados de mais de 600 mil pessoas ao longo de quase 30 anos
articles.summary: A maior pesquisa sobre inteligência emocional, com 600 mil pessoas, revela como a prática e a socialização explicam a vantagem feminina nessa habilidade ao longo das décadas.
articles.body:
Apesar de os dados indicarem uma superioridade feminina em inteligência emocional, eles também mostram que é uma habilidade moldada pela prática, que também faz dela um potencial inexplorado pelos homens. — Foto: PeopleImages/Shutterstock

Quem vem à sua mente quando você pensa em alguém emocionalmente inteligente? Alguém capaz de perceber o clima de um ambiente, acalmar uma discussão e que sabe exatamente o que dizer quando um amigo está passando por dificuldades? Para muitas pessoas, essa pessoa é uma mulher. Essa crença é tão difundida que a psicologia popular a trata como um fato.

Decidimos assim colocar essa suposição à prova. Nosso novo estudo analisou quase três décadas de pesquisas, de 1995 a 2023, em 76 países e com mais de 600 mil pessoas. Queríamos responder a uma pergunta simples: as mulheres são realmente mais inteligentes emocionalmente do que os homens? A resposta principal é sim: em média, as mulheres obtêm pontuação mais alta de inteligência emocional que os homens.

Mas a descoberta mais útil é o tipo de inteligência emocional em que as mulheres parecem se destacar e o que isso pode custar às pessoas que a possuem.

Inteligência emocional é a capacidade de reconhecer, compreender e regular as emoções em si mesmo e nos outros. Ao analisarmos cada elemento da inteligência emocional, verificamos que a vantagem feminina se concentrava na parte da equação relacionada aos “sentimentos dos outros”.

Isso significa reconhecer o que outra pessoa está sentindo, compreender o motivo e ajudá-la a lidar com isso. Uma criança tem uma crise de choro, um colega fica em silêncio depois que sua ideia é rejeitada em uma reunião, uma negociação fica tensa. Muitos homens também são excelentes nisso, e muitas mulheres não são. Nosso estudo traz médias calculadas a partir de centenas de milhares de pessoas, não previsões sobre qualquer pessoa específica na sala.

Mas essa diferença se deve simplesmente à biologia? Não podemos descartar totalmente os fatores biológicos ou hormonais. Mas dois padrões em nossos dados apontam para outra direção. A vantagem feminina é muito menor em crianças do que em adultos, e essa diferença vem diminuindo ao longo das três décadas abrangidas por nossos dados. Isso não é o que se esperaria de algo determinado desde o nascimento. Embora os dados de nosso estudo não possam nos indicar as razões exatas pelas quais essas diferenças surgem, esse padrão se alinha ao que se esperaria de algo moldado pela prática.

Há também uma origem plausível para essa prática. Outras pesquisas descobriram que os pais usam um vocabulário mais amplo de palavras relacionadas a emoções com as filhas do que com os filhos , e com mais frequência incentivam as meninas a refletir sobre seus sentimentos e a expressá-los.

Os meninos, por sua vez, são mais frequentemente orientados a lidar com as emoções suprimindo-as . Suas irmãs são incentivadas a lidar com isso junto com outras pessoas — exatamente o tipo de habilidade social e emocional na qual, segundo nossos dados, as mulheres se destacam.

Em termos simples, as meninas desde cedo parecem ter mais prática em interpretar e responder às emoções alheias. Como qualquer habilidade desenvolvida por meio da repetição, seja aprender um novo idioma ou tocar um novo instrumento, quanto mais você pratica, mais natural ela se torna.

De fato, uma meta-análise de 2019 com 58 estudos constatou que a inteligência emocional pode ser treinada . O gênero não pareceu afetar a eficácia do aprendizado de como ser mais inteligente emocionalmente.

Essa é uma boa notícia. Se a inteligência emocional é uma habilidade que pode ser treinada em vez de um traço fixo, a diferença entre os sexos não é um destino inevitável. Isso significa que os homens também podem se beneficiar dessas habilidades, inclusive em negociações e no trabalho.

Mas há também uma implicação menos confortável. Se a vantagem das mulheres nesse aspecto não for reconhecida como uma habilidade e for tratada, em vez disso, como “algo próprio das mulheres”, torna-se muito fácil considerá-la algo natural. A colega que é boa em amenizar tensões passa a ser aquela de quem sempre se espera que faça isso. Uma capacidade transforma-se silenciosamente em uma obrigação: não remunerada e sem recompensa.

Isso ocorre no ambiente de trabalho todos os dias. As organizações se beneficiam quando as funcionárias lidam com a tensão na equipe, apoiam colegas estressados e amenizam conflitos. É um trabalho que mantém a equipe funcionando, mas que quase nunca aparece em uma avaliação de desempenho.

Duas mudanças práticas precisam acompanhar as conclusões do nosso estudo. Primeiro, os empregadores devem nomear esse trabalho e recompensá-lo, tanto nas avaliações quanto nas decisões de promoção. Segundo, investir no desenvolvimento dessas habilidades em todos os funcionários.

A mesma lógica se aplica fora do escritório. Nas famílias e nas amizades, a pessoa que se lembra de que um amigo está tendo uma semana ruim e entra em contato sem que lhe peçam, que percebe quando alguém para de responder no chat em grupo, que sempre pergunta a um membro da família como foi o dia, também está realizando um trabalho real, e esse trabalho é frequentemente dado como certo justamente porque parece não exigir esforço.

Nada disso significa que as mulheres não tenham um ponto forte real nessa área. Nossos dados mostram uma vantagem feminina nas habilidades emocionais. Mas um ponto forte que é dado como certo em vez de treinado, e esperado em vez de compartilhado, não é algo que deva ser reforçado. É um potencial inexplorado para os homens. A pessoa a quem todos recorrem quando as coisas ficam difíceis não tem sorte nem é simplesmente assim por natureza: provavelmente teve mais prática.

O que não fizemos foi dar a todos os outros essa mesma oportunidade ou incentivo para praticar, nem deixar claro que a inteligência emocional era uma habilidade que valia a pena desenvolver desde o início.

Mary M. Hausfeld é professora Assistente de Gestão na Universidade de Limerick.

Jochen Menges é diretor do Centro de Liderança no Futuro do Trabalho na Universidade de Zurique

articles.title: Club manager, aides beat Delhi man to death for spilling beer on his wife: How minor collision ended in murder
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A 29-year-old driver was allegedly beaten to death by a club manager, his wife and three bouncers in north Delhi’s Sarai Rohilla after a party
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A 29-year-old driver was allegedly beaten to death by a club manager, his wife and three bouncers in north Delhi’s Sarai Rohilla after a party turned violent in the early hours of Sunday.The man had gone to the club with friends when he allegedly spilled beer on the manager’s wife, who was celebrating her birthday, triggering an argument. Police held five people, including the club manager, his wife and a bouncer, within hours of the incident. The deceased, Daljeet Singh, a resident of JJ Colony in Raghubir Nagar, visited the club on New Rohtak Road in Inderlok in north Delhi around 3.30 am on Oct 11 with five friends, Pawan, Arbaz Ali, Ashu, Tinu and Gautam.During the altercation, Daljeet and his friends were allegedly assaulted by the club staff. The group later returned to their respective homes in Raghubir Nagar. After reaching home, Daljeet vomited and went to sleep, police said.His condition deteriorated around noon Sunday, after which his wife, Puja, took him to Guru Gobind Singh Hospital in Khayala, where doctors pronounced him dead. Later, a PCR call was made around 6.52 pm on Sunday.Police subsequently received information about the death from the hospital and verified the circumstances surrounding the incident. The alleged assault was captured on CCTV cameras.How Minor Collision Ended In MurderBouncers Attacked Driver For An Hour: FriendPolice have registered an FIR under multiple sections of BNS including for murder, attempt to murder, voluntarily causing hurt, wrongful confinement, and criminal intimidation involving serious threats. Sections under Cigarettes and Other Tobacco Products Act (COTPA) were also included.The five arrested accused have been identified as Dilawar alias Hasnain, a guest organiser; Sunny alias Gaurav, the club manager; Sharvan Kumar, who was responsible for checking entries at the main gate; bouncer Vikash Balyan; and Harshita, the manager’s wife, whose birthday was being celebrated at the club, according to police. Investigators alleged that Sharvan assaulted Daljeet while another person was taking him back.Meanwhile, the in charge of Inderlok police post has been sent to District Lines for alleged dereliction of duty after the club was found operating until the early hours of the morning, police said. Sources said the club had remained open until at least 5 am.Daljeet worked as a driver and was the sole breadwinner for his family, a friend said. He is survived by his wife, an eight-year-old son and a younger brother.Tinu, one of Daljeet’s friends who was present at the club, said the group had been enjoying themselves when a minor collision caused beer to spill on the manager’s wife.Another friend alleged that Daljeet was hit on his stomach, legs and head during the assault. This prompted the group to intervene. The situation soon escalated when bouncers joined the altercation, he claimed. articles.title: Lena Dunham's Girls returning for limited run at HBO
articles.summary: Ten years after the series finale, the "Girls" are getting back together to explore the "milestone of turning forty", HBO says.
articles.body:
HBO's award-winning show Girls will return to screens for a limited run ten years after the series finale aired.

Lena Dunham – the show's creator, writer, and one of its stars – shared the announcement in a mock zoom call with members of the original cast Allison Williams, Jemima Kirke, Zosia Mamet and Andrew Rannells.

All five actors, whose careers launched off the back of Girls, will be part of the five-episode revival with production set to begin in 2027. Judd Apatow, who helped get the show green lit with HBO, will also return as executive producer.

"We always said we would only return to 'Girls' if there was a specific story we were burning to tell," Dunham said in a statement.

"I've missed these characters, but for a long time I couldn't quite picture them in the present day," she said.

"Then, right around my 40th birthday, they started talking to me in the shower. And, as you may remember, once this fivesome starts talking it's pretty hard to get them to stop," she said.

Girls, which ran for six seasons from 2012 to 2017, was nominated for 19 Emmys and won two, including best casting.

It follows the lives of four friends – Hannah, played by Dunham, Marnie, played by Williams, Jessa, played by Kirke and Shoshanna, played by Mamet – living in New York City during their 20s.

The show, created by Dunham when she was 23-years-old, attracted both praise and controversy during its airing. The BBC ranked it as number 30 on its 100 Greatest TV Shows of the 21st Century.

"We're thrilled to have Lena turn her gaze from the tumult of one's twenties to the milestone of turning forty," Amy Gravitt, executive vice-president of HBO programming, said.

"To say the world has changed since we last saw Hannah, Marnie, Shoshanna, Jessa, and Elijah is a massive understatement, but we know fans - old and new - will be happy to see how they've grown and relieved to see that they're still the 'Girls' we knew way back when."

The title of the limited run has yet to be announced, but Dunham did ask her fellow cast on the mock zoom call, "can we still call it Girls?", before joking "because we're old as".

Other cast and production members, most notably actor Adam Driver, were absent from HBO's official statement. Driver, in his breakout role, played Dunham's on-and-off again love interest in the show.

In her 2026 bestselling memoir Famesick, Dunham alleged Driver's on-set behaviour at times turned verbally aggressive and physically imposing. Driver has not publicly commented on the allegations.

In Famesick, Dunham also wrote about the breakdown of her working relationship and friendship with co-showrunner and executive producer Jenni Konner. Konner is not included in HBO's statement about the show's revival.

Dunham wrote on her Substack that "it's rare in life that you get the chance to return to something you love with new knowledge and a ... ton of gratitude.

"I love these girls (and boy) and I love all the people who have reminded us afresh why we do this, which is the joy of being together and the chance to wear yellow mesh…" she wrote.

Since Girls ended, Dunham has gone on to create the Netflix series Too Much in 2025 and indie film Sharp Stick.

articles.summary: Iran is changing its tactics to step up attacks on commercial shipping in the Gulf and keep global oil prices elevated ahead of the November 3 US midterm
articles.body: Iran is changing its tactics to step up attacks on commercial shipping in the Gulf and keep global oil prices elevated ahead of the November 3 US midterm elections. This comes as Tehran seeks to increase economic pressure on US President Donald Trump.“The aim is to frustrate efforts by the United States and its allies to bring down global oil prices,” news agency Reuters quoted one Iranian official saying. The official added that the strategy had been approved at the highest levels of Iran's leadership.The official said Tehran would seek to push prices higher whenever Washington appeared close to bringing them down.“Just when they think they are getting close to the point where prices will fall, we will push them away from it. In a previously unreported incident, US forces identified spotters operating from a traditional dhow and relaying targeting information to the IRGC.The Iranian officials also said Iran intended to expand its operations beyond the Strait of Hormuz to the Gulf of Oman and waters further afield, including areas off Qatar and the United Arab Emirates.“Such vessels would be safe nowhere, even outside the Strait of Hormuz,” the official said, warning that ships violating Iran's restrictions could face threats beyond the strategic waterway.The strategy could complicate Trump's efforts to ease energy costs ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, in which control of Congress is at stake.Sustained disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz could keep oil prices elevated, increasing fuel costs for American consumers and adding to economic pressure on the administration.Higher energy prices could also give Trump's political opponents an opportunity to criticise his handling of the conflict and its economic consequences.You use AI every day. The blaze was brought under control after nearly six hours. articles.title: Ukrainian ex-officer goes on trial in Germany over Nord Stream blasts
articles.summary: The trial is expected to run into February and could test Germany’s political stance on Ukraine.
articles.body:
A Ukrainian former military officer is standing trial in Germany, accused of organising the secret operation that blew up the Nord Stream gas pipelines in 2022 and cut Western Europe off from its biggest source of Russian natural gas.

The trial opened on Wednesday at the Hamburg Higher Regional Court and is expected to run into February next year.

It is the first public hearing of the evidence in a years-long investigation.

The defendant, a 50-year-old identified under German privacy rules only as Serhii K., is accused of leading a group of Ukrainian agents – including divers and an explosives expert – in one of the biggest infrastructure sabotage operations of modern times.

He denies any involvement and is the only person on trial.

Serhii K. was arrested in Italy in August 2025 and extradited to Germany that November.

Prosecutors accused him of working with other members of the military to plan the operation on behalf of unidentified Ukrainian state entities.

They allege he travelled to Germany through Poland on a forged Ukrainian passport about three weeks before the attack.

They say the group used a sailboat hired in the northern city of Rostock to reach an area near the Danish island of Bornholm, where they attached military-grade explosives with timers to the pipelines on the seabed.

German prosecutors say attacking civilian targets and destroying infrastructure in this way would amount to a war crime.

On September 26, 2022, Swedish seismologists detected several blasts, some 17 hours apart.

Three of the four concrete-coated steel pipelines ruptured, sending huge plumes of methane into the atmosphere.

Nord Stream 1 had supplied about half of Germany’s natural gas imports. Its twin, Nord Stream 2, was built but never opened, after Berlin cancelled approval shortly before Russia invaded Ukraine.

Moscow denied blowing up its own pipelines and had already cut supplies in response to European sanctions.

Ukraine’s government denies involvement.

Russia said on Monday it expected a “just verdict” naming the perpetrators and those who ordered the operation.

Another suspect, Vladimir Z., a trained scuba diver who prosecutors say was one of the divers on the team, was arrested in Croatia in August.

Last month, a Croatian court approved handing over the wanted man to Germany.

The Nord Stream case has strained ties between Berlin and Kyiv, even as Germany remains one of Ukraine’s strongest backers, with Russia and Ukraine still trading strikes.

articles.title: Israel returns 22 stolen ancient artefacts to Greece
articles.summary: The cultural exchange comes amid strengthening ties between the two countries.
articles.body:
Israel has returned 22 ancient artefacts stolen from Greece, a cultural exchange that comes as the two countries strengthen ties.

Greek and Israeli officials did not provide details on Tuesday on how the artefacts were discovered in Israel or the circumstances surrounding their illegal removal from Greece.

The Israel Antiquities Authority’s Theft Prevention Unit had located the items, Pninat Yanay, Israel’s ambassador to Greece, said.

Greek Minister of Culture Lina Mendoni accepted the objects from the Israeli Antiquities Authority at a ceremony held at the National Archaeological Museum in Athens.

“It is the first time that Israel has returned antiquities to Greece, marking the starting point of closer cooperation between the two countries for the protection of cultural heritage,” Mendoni said.

“Every return of a cultural object to its place of origin has a broader symbolic and moral dimension.”

The collection includes 15 Attic vases, six Corinthian vases, and a bronze female statuette.

The objects are dated between 700 BC and 320 BC.

Yanay said the return of the antiquities created “the conditions for further strengthening cooperation between Greece and Israel”.

Greece and Israel have strengthened energy and defence ties in recent years.

In August, Israel signed a $3.5bn defence deal to build a multi-layered air defence system in Greece, called the Achilles Shield. It is the largest defence deal between the two countries, and one of the most significant export agreements in Israel’s recent history.

articles.title: A rare Ten Commandments tablet was reportedly used as a paving stone for decades; it sold for $5.04 million despite doubts over its origins
articles.summary: A rare stone tablet inscribed with the Ten Commandments sold for $5.04 million at a Sotheby’s auction in New York on 18 December 2024, decades after it
articles.body: A rare stone tablet inscribed with the Ten Commandments sold for $5.04 million at a Sotheby’s auction in New York on 18 December 2024, decades after it was reportedly used as a paving stone. According to The New York Times, the tablet was discovered during railway construction near the coast of what is now southern Israel in 1913, but its historical significance was not recognised immediately. Sotheby’s dated the 115-pound artefact to the late Roman-Byzantine period, around 1,500 years ago. However, experts questioned its provenance and authenticity because its discovery lacked independently verifiable archaeological documentation.How was the rare Ten Commandments tablet discovered in 1913The tablet’s discovery dates back to 1913, when a railway was being built near the coast of what is now southern Israel. Jacob Kaplan, who later investigated the stone, reported that it had been found during the construction work. Rather than being immediately recognised as an important historical artefact, the inscribed stone was reportedly used as a paving stone at a nearby home, with its inscription facing upwards as it was set into the ground.Kaplan published his findings in 1947 in The Bulletin of the Jewish Palestine Exploration Society, a scholarly journal. He died in 1989. The account of the discovery subsequently became part of the tablet’s documented history, although experts later questioned whether the reported circumstances could be independently verified. The absence of archaeological excavation records from 1913 became a central issue in discussions about the stone’s authenticity.How did the Ten Commandments tablet reach Sotheby’s auctionThe tablet eventually entered the antiquities market. It reached an Israeli antiquities dealer in 1995 before being acquired by the Living Torah Museum in Brooklyn. In 2016, collector Mitchell S. Cappell purchased it for $850,000. Cappell later consigned the stone to Sotheby’s, where it was auctioned in December 2024.Sotheby’s described the tablet as approximately 1,500 years old and associated it with the late Roman-Byzantine period. The stone weighs 115 pounds, measures two feet in length and bears an inscription in Paleo-Hebrew, an early form of Hebrew writing. The auction house cited the lettering, wear and weathering as evidence relevant to determining its age. Selby Kiffer, Sotheby’s international senior specialist for books and manuscripts, highlighted the importance of the script, stating, “The script is a key to it. We know when it went out of common usage.”Why have experts questioned the authenticity of the tabletDespite Sotheby’s claims about the tablet’s age and significance, specialists raised concerns about its provenance, meaning the documented history of an object’s ownership and discovery. Patty Gerstenblith, director of the Centre for Art, Museum and Cultural Heritage Law at DePaul University College of Law, described the auction result as “remarkable” but emphasised that doubts about the artefact needed serious consideration.In an email quoted by The New York Times, Gerstenblith said, “The inscription has no objectively verifiable origin, such as discovery during a documented archaeological excavation.” She also questioned aspects of the discovery account, noting that “Several elements of the story, such as that its significance was unrecognised for several decades, seem to stretch belief.” Her concerns centred on the lack of independently verifiable archaeological evidence establishing when and where the tablet was originally found.Brian I. Daniels, director of research and programmes at the Penn Cultural Heritage Centre in Philadelphia, also highlighted the risks associated with antiquities from the region. He said, “Objects from this region of the world are rife with fakes.” However, he acknowledged that the tablet could still prove genuine, adding, “Maybe it’s absolutely authentic, and this truly is a historic find.”Christopher A. Rollston, chairman of the Department of Classical and Near Eastern Languages and Civilisations at George Washington University, questioned whether the stone could reliably be dated to the late Roman-Byzantine period. He said that it was possible the tablet had been carved closer to the time of its reported discovery, rather than centuries earlier. “But there is no way that this can be known,” Rollston said in an email quoted by The New York Times. He added, “After all, these were not found on an archaeological excavation. We don’t even know who actually found them.”Rollston also challenged the account that the tablet had been used as a paving stone after its discovery in 1913. He pointed to the absence of contemporary records and the possibility that stories about an object's discovery could be fabricated to make it appear more authentic. “The problem is that we have zero documentation from 1913, and since pillagers and forgers often concoct such stories to give an inscription an aura of authenticity, this story could actually just be a tall tale told by a forger or some antiquities dealer,” he said.How does the tablet differ from the traditional versionThe tablet contains a version of the Ten Commandments that differs in certain respects from the wording commonly known today. It omits the prohibition against taking the Lord’s name in vain and includes an instruction to worship on Mount Gerizim, a sacred site for the Samaritans in what is now the West Bank.Rollston specifically questioned the inclusion of the Mount Gerizim directive, suggesting that unusual details can sometimes be introduced into forged inscriptions to attract interest. He said, “Forgers during the past 150 years, when they fabricate their forgeries, often throw in surprising content.” He added, “And they do this to garner more interest in their forgery.” These concerns formed part of the wider debate over whether the tablet’s inscription reflected an ancient religious tradition or a later fabrication.Sotheby’s, meanwhile, defended the research conducted on the artefact. Sharon Liberman Mintz, the auction house’s international senior specialist in Judaica, books and manuscripts, said the tablet had been “widely studied, researched, and published by the world’s leading scholars.” She described its significance as undisputed and welcomed the prospect of it being preserved in an Israeli institution. The Israel Antiquities Authority was also pleased that the artefact would return to Israel.How much did the tablet sell for at Sotheby’s auctionThe anonymous buyer who purchased the tablet at Sotheby’s planned to donate it to an Israeli institution, according to the auction house. Sotheby’s said the artefact would have a home where it could be preserved and continue to be studied. Its sale followed more than 10 minutes of bidding and exceeded the auction house’s original estimate of $1 million to $2 million.The auction established the price paid for the tablet, but the questions surrounding its origins remained a separate matter. While Sotheby’s presented it as an exceptionally significant religious artefact and cited its inscription, physical condition and scholarly research, experts highlighted the lack of independently documented archaeological evidence. The stone’s journey from its reported use as a paving stone to a multimillion-dollar auction therefore remains closely linked to both its historical claims and the continuing debate over its authenticity.You use AI every day. articles.title: Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar has an 'AI theory' for more researchers taking up smoking; says: These folks in Silicon Valley have filled hole in their hearts with God of ...
articles.summary: Palantir chief technology officer Shyam Sankar has an unusual explanation for why some AI researchers are picking up cigarettes.
articles.body: Palantir chief technology officer Shyam Sankar has an unusual explanation for why some AI researchers are picking up cigarettes. According to him, lighting up is their way of telling peers just how firmly they believe artificial intelligence will one day cure cancer. Sankar made the remark in a US television interview on Sunday, while arguing that fear-driven narratives are muddying the AI safety debate. He did not name any researchers or offer evidence. "So many AI researchers have started smoking as a way of signaling to other researchers how much they believe in AI," he said. The smoker's message, in his words, is: "I'm showing you my chips are all in."The claim was part of a bigger argument. Citing philosopher Blaise Pascal's idea that every human has a "god-shaped hole" in their heart, Sankar said many people building this technology in Silicon Valley "have filled that hole with the machine God of AGI." He called the mood around it a "mass psychosis."Shyam Sankar blames effective altruism for AI doomsday fearsSankar traced much of the AI anxiety to effective altruism, which he described as a "doomsday cult." Its most famous follower, he noted, is jailed crypto founder Sam Bankman-Fried. By his count, America has roughly 2,000 AI researchers, and most of them share that worldview.So when a researcher like Jacob Coxon warns that AI has a 10% chance of ending humanity, Sankar wants people to treat it as a theological critique rather than a scientific one. He also pointed out that doomsayers once called GPT-2 too dangerous to release and predicted mass unemployment that has not arrived.Palantir CTO wants existing laws to govern how AI is usedSankar insisted he is not against guardrails. He wants rules aimed at how AI is applied, with the FDA watching over medicine and the Department of Transportation over transport. His analogy: a defective car is the carmaker's problem, but driving it into a neighbour's house is yours.He also noted that some frontier models are now being held back from release, which he said would have been unthinkable a year ago.The smoking claim, for now, rests on his word. A small circle of tech founders and investors has embraced cigarettes, and Avi Schiffmann, founder of AI wearable startup Friend, has said AI should have cured lung cancer by the time smokers get it. Medicine is yet to share that confidence. Smoking remains a leading cause of preventable death worldwide.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Russia arrests Japanese journalist for alleged espionage
articles.summary: The Hokkaido Shimbun journalist is accused of collecting information on Moscow's defence capabilities for Tokyo.
articles.body:
Russian authorities have arrested a Japanese journalist on suspicion of espionage, accusing him of gathering information related to Moscow's defence capabilities for Tokyo.

The journalist, identified as Yuki Imai from the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper, was detained in far eastern Sakhalin region, a day before he was due to leave Russia. He was flown to Moscow where a court ordered he be placed in pre-trial detention, Russian reports say.

Japan says it is still seeking details about the arrest, and has not been able to contact him.

The arrest comes as tensions worsen between the two nations after Russian leader Vladimir Putin visited the disputed Kuril Islands , claimed by both countries, in August.

Russian authorities allege that Imai "acted on the instructions of [Japan's] national intelligence service" to gather information about people involved in a special military operation on the Kuril Islands, state news agency TASS reported.

The Kuril islands sit between Hokkaido in northern Japan and Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula. The archipelago is administered by Russia, but four of the southernmost islands are claimed by Japan, which calls them the Northern Territories.

Imai has been taken to Moscow and will be remanded until 12 December, before his trial begins, according to Interfax, another Russian news agency.

Those convicted of espionage in Russia can be sentenced to up to 20 years in prison.

"Tokyo's attempts to use its correspondents in Russia, who hold foreign journalist status, to gather information aimed at undermining our country's security are regrettable," Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said in a statement on Tuesday.

"We cannot help but point out that today's incident is not an isolated one," she noted, but did not name other journalists or media outlets that are allegedly involved in similar activity.

Japan has not commented at length on the arrest. On Tuesday, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said authorities are "verifying the facts" and will "respond appropriately" thereafter.

Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara told a press briefing that Japan did not know about the arrest until the announcement and had had no contact yet with the journalist.

Imai's published work has covered Russia's relations with North Korea and life in Sakhalin.

Hokkaido Shimbun ran a report on the arrest without naming the reporter. "We are still confirming the details. Ensuring the reporter's safety is our top priority," it said in response to the BBC's queries.

Russia and Japan have been locked in a dispute over the Kurils for decades, and it is the main reason Moscow and Tokyo did not sign a peace treaty after World War Two.

Takaichi sharply criticised Putin's visit – his first-ever to the islands – saying it "wounded the feelings of the Japanese people" and is "incompatible with Japan's consistent position on the Northern Territories".

Moscow dismissed her remarks as "politically inappropriate" and "legally unfounded".

Over the years, attempts to resolve the territorial dispute have made little progress. Bilateral ties have also remained frosty, with Japan imposing sanctions against Russia for its invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Last week, Moscow again angered Tokyo by requesting the extradition of the president of the International Criminal Court (ICC), who is Japanese.

The president Tomoko Akane, along with other ICC officials, has been placed on Russia's wanted list since 2023 after the court issued an arrest warrant for Putin over war crimes in Ukraine.

In 2023, Russia detained The Wall Street Journal's Evan Gershkovich on espionage charges and later sentenced him to 16 years in prison.

Gershkovich, a US citizen, was released in a 2024 prisoner swap, the largest exchange since the Cold War ended in 1991.

In 2019, Moscow detained an unnamed Japanese journalist from Kyodo News on suspicion of attempting to obtain military secrets. The journalist, who was picked up in Vladivostok, was ordered to leave the country within 72 hours.

articles.title: Is asking wife to wash clothes and utensils cruelty? Bombay HC explains Section 498A
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Can asking a woman to wash clothes and utensils at a relative’s house amount to cruelty under Section 498A of the Indian Penal Code (IPC)?
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Can asking a woman to wash clothes and utensils at a relative’s house amount to cruelty under Section 498A of the Indian Penal Code (IPC)? The Bombay high court has held that such an act, even if the allegation is assumed to be true, does not by itself constitute cruelty under the provision. The court also quashed a criminal case against six relatives of the husband, finding that the allegations against them were vague and did not specify their individual roles.In an October 1, 2026, order, the high court said the allegations did not disclose enough grounds to continue the proceedings against the six relatives under Section 498A of the IPC.What were the allegations against the husband’s relatives?According to the court order, the woman alleged that her husband and his relatives taunted her for being unable to conceive a child and subjected her to mental and physical harassment. She also alleged that her husband had taken her to a relative’s house, where she was asked to wash clothes and utensils.The six relatives approached the high court seeking to quash the FIR and the criminal proceedings against them. They also argued that the allegations were vague and did not specify the role played by each of them. They further claimed that they lived in different places, while the woman resided with her husband in Pune.Can relatives be prosecuted for cruelty based on general allegations?Justice Abhay Mantri found that the allegations did not specify the time, date, place or manner of the alleged harassment. The court also noted that the woman’s in-laws lived in different cities and that she visited their homes only occasionally.“The allegations against the Petitioners are vague, omnibus and general in nature,” Justice Mantri observed.The court specifically examined the allegation that the woman had been asked to wash clothes and utensils at a relative’s house. It held that even if she had been asked to do these household chores, the act did not constitute cruelty within the meaning of Section 498A of the IPC.“Apart from that, even assuming that she was asked to wash clothes and utensils, such an act does not constitute the ingredients of Section 498-A of the IPC and cannot be termed as cruelty within the meaning of Section 498-A of the IPC,” the high court said.The court also pointed out that the complaint lacked details about the alleged harassment.“Moreover, Respondent No. 2 has not mentioned the time, date, place or manner in which the alleged harassment occurred. Thus, the FIR and the entire charge-sheet fail to disclose the commission of an offence punishable under Section 498-A of the IPC against the present Petitioners,” it added.The court referred to Supreme Court rulings, including Kahkashan Kausar v State of Bihar (2022), which emphasise the need to carefully scrutinise allegations against a husband’s relatives, particularly when they live separately and are accused through general allegations of harassment.Does living separately protect a husband’s relatives from prosecution?Not automatically. The court’s decision turned on the nature of the allegations and the absence of specific details about the relatives’ alleged conduct. Their separate residence and infrequent contact with the woman were relevant to the court’s assessment of the case.The high court observed that the FIR and charge sheet did not disclose the commission of an offence under Section 498A of the IPC against the six relatives. Continuing the proceedings against them, the court said, would amount to an abuse of the process of law.Final orderThe court quashed the FIR registered at Vijapur Naka police station in Solapur under Sections 498A, 323, 504 and 506 read with Section 34 of the IPC, along with the related criminal case, but only insofar as it concerned the six petitioners.The order did not quash the proceedings against the woman’s husband. The court allowed the petition to that extent and passed no order on costs.

articles.title: Russell T Davies criticises BBC boss's 'clumsy' AI Doctor Who comments
articles.summary: BBC director general Matt Brittin said he had seen a "pretty good" AI-generated episode of the show.
articles.body:
Longtime Doctor Who writer and showrunner Russell T Davies has criticised the new BBC director general over comments he made about an AI-generated episode of the show.

Matt Brittin told a Royal Television Society conference in September that he had been sent a "pretty good" 50-minute unofficial Doctor Who episode.

"That's a clumsy thing to say in an industry where he's got writers and artists and it specifically affects people, they're the first to take the blow," Davies told BBC Radio 4's The Media Show.

Addressing criticism he has received, Brittin told a staff meeting last week he was attempting to make a point around the "pace of change" while stressing he believed in "human creativity".

The director general joked he had "got into trouble" over what he had said, but added: "I was just trying to make the point: Look at the pace of change and what this stuff can do."

He said: "I want to be really clear: Humans are leading, and I believe in human creativity, enhanced by whatever tools."

He emphasised human-led creativity would always be at the heart of the BBC's mission.

But speaking to BBC Radio 4, Davies said that the new director general, who joined the BBC after a career at Google, "hasn't worked in television for that long and might not be so fruity with an opinion in future".

"My inbox went ping ping ping ping ping, so God knows what his was like," he added.

Davies was also asked more broadly about AI, including how, or if, writers should use the technology.

"I have heard stories of some writers using AI prompts to do a first draft which I find shocking because I think... What are you paid for otherwise? What are you there to do?"

He said he did not use it to write his scripts but he "very much" worried it would start to replace writers, and in some circumstances that may already be the case.

Davies is one of the UK's most influential television writers - from the ground-breaking Queer as Folk to acclaimed dramas including It's a Sin, Years and Years and, more recently, Tip Toe, he has had a major impact on British TV.

But perhaps his most significant achievement is his work on Doctor Who.

In 2005, he brought the Timelord back after a 16-year absence after pitching it to the BBC's then-head of drama at a party in Manchester.

He revived the show again in 2023, although he confirmed earlier this year he would be stepping away.

He told The Media Show there were times he "used to dread going on a Doctor Who set" because of the expensive special effects and "explosions going on, people pulling themselves in to prosthetics".

"It's more difficult than any other set."

The BBC cancelled the planned Christmas special and Disney+ no longer co-finances the series.

But Davies had good news for Doctor Who fans. Another series is on the cards, he promised, even though he will not be involved.

"You'll start to see production with a brand-new Doctor, a brand-new companion, summer next year."

Davies - who recently released his memoir 'The Queerest of Folk: A Life in Television' - got his first break aged 22 working in BBC children's TV "for £50 a day".

"It was the best training you could possibly have," he said.

The Swansea-born writer later honed his skills in the heyday of Granada Television "when Coronation Street was getting 18 million, 20 million [views]".

Also in the interview, he revealed inspiration can come from the most unlikely sources - he "records the phone-ins on This Morning" and listens to them in the evening.

"All human life is there… just a couple of times a year, you'll get an extraordinary human story or something very funny. One of my favourite ones about a year ago was a woman whose mother-in-law was insisting on wearing white to her wedding".

He believes he will get a script out of that "one day": "What a great little problem that is - two women just at war."

Russell T Davies' interview will be on The Media Show, Wednesday 4.15pm BBC Radio 4 & BBC Sounds

articles.title: World's oldest shipwreck found off Kekova Island in Turkey
articles.summary: Archaeologists say the wreck is up to 4,700 years old, dating to the Early Bronze Age.
articles.body:
The world's oldest shipwreck has been discovered off the coast of Turkey, archaeologists say.

They have dated it to between 4,400 and 4,700 years old, which is the Early Bronze Age, and is around the same time that the Great Pyramid was being built.

The ship's wooden structure has not survived, but the ceramic storage pots it was carrying were lying on the sea floor and, remarkably, some still contain traces of what they held inside.

The archaeologists who found the ship say it was about 10m in length and was a trade vessel carrying cargo across the Mediterranean Sea.

"The shipwreck is a time capsule at the bottom of the sea," said Prof Hakan Öniz, from Akdeniz University in Turkey, who led the Mediterranean Archaeology Association expedition.

The wreck is close to the shore of Kekova Island in Antalya, Turkey. The artefacts lie scattered across an underwater slope, just 30m beneath the waves.

Three large stone anchors were found, as well as more than 30 ceramic storage pots, called amphorae.

The fact that none of the ship's wood remained meant techniques like radiocarbon dating - which measures a form of carbon in organic materials - could not be used to determine its age.

Instead, archaeologists analysed the shape of the amphorae. Because pottery styles have changed over time, differerent styles are linked to particular periods.

The Kekova ceramics are distinctive, with two handles, a ridge in the middle and a flat base.

Öniz said this design matched other amphorae unearthed in Egypt and the Middle East that were known to be 4,400-4,700 years old.

"Comparing the decoration techniques… we can definitely say our wreck is Early Bronze Age. This is 100%."

Divers from the expedition brought the pots up to the surface, where they are now being carefully conserved after so many thousands of years underwater.

Dr Karin Sowada, an archaeologist from Macquarie University, Australia, examined the amphorae after they were recovered. Some were intact and she was surprised to see they still contained a viscous, glossy residue.

"I looked inside and nearly fainted. I could not believe how much [residue] was visible. It wasn't just like spots…. a lot of this material was still remaining," she said.

The team is now working to find out exactly what was being carried in the amphorae.

"It could be olive oil, it could be wine, it could be tree resins," Sowada said.

"It's possible that [the residue] could actually be the result of reuse of the jars. I mean, these jars are huge - they're not things that you just ship away and then never see again. People would have emptied these jars on arrival and potentially used them for many, many, many years."

The wreck and its cargo are also shedding light on trade in the ancient world.

The archaeologists say the ship started its voyage from somewhere along the eastern coast of the Mediterranean.

They believe it was taking goods to either the ancient city of Troy, in what is now north-western Turkey, or to the Minoan people in Crete.

Travelling by sea was fraught with danger, particularly around Kekova Island, where the strong currents and winds have claimed many ships.

There are hundreds of wrecks in the area, and the Mediterranean Archaelogy Association specialises in finding and studying them.

Öniz says that when he is diving on the wreck his first thoughts are about the lives of the people who were connected to this vessel.

"We are the first humans who [have] touched these objects after 5,000 years.

"We are always thinking of the sailors... the producers of the amphora and the person who carried the amphora on their shoulders to the ship, and the women who were waiting for their husbands, and they unfortunately couldn't go back."

The Kekova discovery now tops the list of the world's oldest shipwrecks.

Previously, the record holder was a wreck off the coast of Dokos, an island in southern Greece, which dates to about 4,200 years ago.

The oldest known shipwreck where some of the wood is still preserved was found in the Black Sea off the coast of Bulgaria. It dates to about 2,400 years ago.

articles.title: One stolen every four minutes - inside the police battle against vehicle thieves
articles.summary: Officers tell the BBC they are overstretched and struggling to keep up with sophisticated criminals.
articles.body:
It is 01:00 on a Thursday and we are in the back of an unmarked police car on the hunt for vehicle thieves in east London.

A call comes in over the radio about a stolen Ford Transit van. Within 25 minutes officers have found it, chased it down and arrested a suspect.

Officers tell us the night has been successful, with further arrests made, yet across the UK a car is stolen every four minutes.

Despite a recent drop, vehicle thefts are up almost 50% in England and Wales compared with a decade ago, according to Home Office data. Last year, just 3% of vehicle theft offences resulted in a charge or summons.

As well as spending time on the front line in London and Sussex, we have privately spoken to 20 police officers from six forces.

They told us while they have the skills and experience to tackle vehicle crime, they are overstretched, under-resourced and struggling to keep pace with increasingly sophisticated criminal networks.

Thieves are becoming more confident. A man who claims he receives stolen vehicles and breaks them into parts at a so-called "chop shop" told the BBC he does not fear the authorities, because they "couldn't catch a cold".

Once the preserve of joyriders and opportunists, vehicle theft is now a lucrative global criminal business. Cars are stolen to order, and moved across the country or dismantled within hours, say police, making them difficult to recover and suspects hard to track. Many vehicles are sent overseas to places like the United Arab Emirates, The Democratic Republic of Congo and Jamaica.

Victims of car theft have told us they feel frustrated and helpless. One woman said it took car thieves just 35 seconds to steal her BMW, yet police only began investigating a day later. Another man said he feared for his life when masked thieves broke into his home demanding his car keys.

The success criminals are having is also hitting motorists more widely, with insurance quotes having risen by 82% since 2021, according to security think tank the Royal United Services Institute (Rusi).

Our night-time ride in the unmarked police car takes place during an eight-hour Metropolitan Police operation targeting vehicle crime.

"Havering has been affected quite badly," PC Yoosef Outaleb tells us - partly because thieves use the back roads as a cut-through to neighbouring Essex.

Police say the county has particularly high numbers of illegal "chop shops", which dismantle vehicles for parts so they can be sold and exported.

"They [the criminals] don't have borders, whereas we do," he says. When criminal activity straddles police force boundaries, investigations can often slow down - which gangs look to exploit.

Two stolen vehicles are recovered, yet Met officers also uncover other crimes.

They pursue armed robbers on e-bikes, apprehend a drunk driver and arrest three men in a car full of Class A drugs, cash and phones.

It is all important work, but police admit that responding to these crimes diverts them away from targeting known vehicle thieves.

The thieves, known as "grafters" within criminal networks, are out every night stealing cars, the man claiming to work at a chop shop told us.

Many vehicles are then broken into parts. Such is the demand, he says, that deals to re-sell the parts are often done before he has even finished dismantling a vehicle.

Some stolen vehicles are left intact, given new number plates and sold in the UK or abroad, while others are used to facilitate drug dealing and human trafficking, or as getaway vehicles for robberies and break-ins.

While the long-term trend presents difficult reading for police, reported vehicle thefts fell 5% in England and Wales last year, to 119,000. In Scotland and Northern Ireland, vehicle thefts remained largely flat, at about 5,000 and 1,200 a year respectively.

Fifteen of the 32 police forces in England and Wales that responded to a BBC Freedom of Information request said they do not employ any full-time, specially-trained stolen vehicle examiners, who can carry out detailed examinations of cars and bolster investigations.

But Assistant Chief Constable Sarah Grahame, the national police lead on tackling vehicle crime, tells us officers' efforts - like the night-time operation in east London - are having an impact.

UK forces are also collaborating with Interpol, shipping companies and vehicle manufacturers to address an issue "that spans globally", she says.

She admits current theft levels are unacceptable, but says there is no funding to routinely carry out large-scale operations within current police budgets, set by the Home Office.

Instead, forces organise "intensification weeks" aimed at disrupting criminal networks.

One involving 32 forces last month, called Operation Alliances, led to at least 286 arrests and 319 vehicles seized.

In East Sussex in September, where we witnessed a smaller, targeted operation, we were told that 17 cars had been stolen in the Hastings and Rother areas in the previous two months.

Many of the vehicles were keyless Toyota RAV4s - taken by thieves using technology that bypasses vehicle security systems. Three of the vehicles had been taken the previous night.

Within hours, officers recovered all three vehicles and arrested three suspects, including one they believe had been in charge of the other two.

Two suspects have now been charged, including one arrested after a stolen Toyota was found near his home.

Sussex vehicle crime lead Ch Insp Oliver Fisher, says police resources are now being focused on "the top of that criminal network... that's where you'll seize the most assets and cause the most disruption".

Without catching criminal bosses, experts agree, others lower down will continue carrying out thefts to order - often using tech such as cloned keys to access vehicles.

Manufacturers need "a constant focus on security", says Thatcham Research - a body that works with carmakers, police and government to improve vehicle security.

"Within months" of a car being launched, thieves can develop targeted tools to steal it, it says.

At Thatcham Research's headquarters, we are shown a device hidden within a wireless speaker that can start a car by tapping into its internal communication system. We also see a military-grade signal jammer, left behind by criminals after a theft, that can block out all electronic signals for miles around.

While manufacturers are meeting security guidelines, the government should update regulations to ensure "sophisticated [theft] countermeasures are on a vehicle as standard", says Thatcham Research's principal engineer for automotive security, Steve Launchbury.

Tech that puts a key to sleep while motionless is one option, he says, so thieves cannot hack into it. In future, it may be possible for manufacturers to remotely lock down a car reported by the owner as stolen, he adds.

The Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders told us car makers go "above and beyond regulatory requirements", while Toyota said it "continuously enhances vehicle security".

Mike, 33, believed he had done everything he could to prevent his BMW M2 from being taken. He had CCTV, a house alarm and a protective container for his keys.

But just two months after he bought the car, two masked men broke into his home in the middle of the night and demanded the keys.

"I was kind of scared for my life," he says. Avon and Somerset Police says it is "following up all lines of enquiry", but his car has not been recovered.

Rose-Marie Clarke has been a victim of car theft twice in three years. Most recently, in March, her BMW was stolen from outside her home using an antenna to amplify the signal from the key fob inside her house. It took thieves just 35 seconds.

Clarke, like many victims we have spoken to, is critical of the police.

She says officers told her they knew the likely suspect, who had recently been released from prison, but they had been unable to prove it was him. "It's disheartening… you feel powerless because the police are powerless," she says.

Warwickshire Police said despite "extensive enquiries… an offender could not be identified". BMW UK said it worked "continuously" to improve security.

Many victims we spoke to told us they had also been hit hard by a rise in their car insurance premiums.

Across the UK, car insurance quotes have risen by 82% since 2021 and Eli Glantz, an expert in organised crime and policing at security think tank Rusi, says vehicle crime "is certainly a factor".

"As more vehicles are stolen, insurers are forced to pay out more often. Premiums are going to rise," he adds.

Vehicle crime costs the UK economy £1.7bn a year, Rusi estimates.

Since April, it has been an offence to possess electronic devices used in vehicle thefts, but Glantz believes legislation is still failing to keep pace with the criminals.

It is welcome, he says, that the government is now giving vehicle thefts more attention, but he stresses that current police resources will not meaningfully reduce the number of crimes.

Several of the police officers we spoke to privately felt similarly. They said they had confidence in their ability to take down serious, organised vehicle crime networks, provided they had the necessary level of funding and support from decision-makers.

The Home Office says it "will continue to support police" in tackling organised vehicle theft and provides £300,000 a year to help strengthen its response, mainly to the National Vehicle Crime Reduction Partnership.

articles.title: Home of London's oldest restaurant Rules given to National Trust
articles.summary: Rules, in Covent Garden, which opened in 1798, will be looked after and conserved by the charity.
articles.body:
The home of London's oldest restaurant, which has hosted famous faces from Charles Dickens to Madonna over the past two centuries, has been given to the National Trust.

Rules originally opened in 1798 at 34-35 Maiden Lane in Covent Garden and has outlasted empires, survived the Blitz and fought off development plans.

The £11m freehold gift of the restaurant building along with its historic collection such as visitor books, menus, photographs will now be protected for future generations, the National Trust said.

Rules restaurant will continue to trade, while becoming a commercial tenant of the charity. Under the deal, the rent payments will go towards conserving the building.

Rules, which has well-preserved interior, has welcomed generations of high profile figures from Charles Dickens to Charlie Chaplin, as well as Edward VII, who would meet with his mistresses there, and stars David Bowie, Liza Minnelli and Harrison Ford.

It was favourite spot for poet John Betjeman, who once gave an impassioned speech in defence of the restaurant when it was under threat of redevelopment.

Writer Graham Greene was known to enjoy birthday meals there and featured it in his novel The End Of The Affair.

Hilary McGrady, director-general of the National Trust, said: "This place is an outstanding piece of living history, with its corners where kings dined and writers and politicians plotted, and the traditions it kept alive through wars and upheaval.

"It has defied the odds to be standing here today, doors still open and treacle sponge still on the menu.

"Mr Mayhew's extraordinary generosity, and the care he has poured into Rules over many decades, mean this beloved place has a future measured not in years but generations."

The building's owner, J-P Mayhew, said: "There are few restaurants in the world that have endured the test of time like Rules.

"The trust will protect this place in a way that no-one else could, safeguarding its bricks and mortar, its famous interior and its invisible atmosphere, too.

"I am grateful to them for believing in this idea and for protecting this building and two centuries' worth of stories for people to enjoy forever."

The restaurant's proprietor Ricky McMenemy, who has worked there for 35 years, will become a commercial tenant of the conservation charity.

He welcomed the donation, saying: "As an independent business, it gives us both the security and peace of mind that our home will be in very good hands and be protected and secure going forward."
