articles.title: Devon and Cornwall theme parks had boost in summer, bosses say
articles.summary: It may have been hot but the attractions saw a rise in visitors over summer, tourism bosses say.
articles.body:
A hot summer has given some tourist attractions a "much-needed boost" after a difficult few years, bosses have said.

Cornwall Visitor Alliance said sunny weather had "really helped" draw people in and spending improved, helping relieve pressure from rising running costs .

Among those reporting a positive season was Crealy Theme and Resort Park in Devon, one of the region's biggest attractions, which is considering how to adapt for the future after the hottest summer on record .

Indoor attractions including the National Marine Aquarium in Plymouth said visitors had come to "escape from the sun" but this was in contrast to Bodmin Jail which reported a "huge decline" in numbers over summer.

Devon Association of Tourist Attractions chairman Roger Sell said visitor numbers varied considerably across the county but spending was generally strong despite lower footfall for indoor attractions, making for a "mixed but resilient summer overall".

The Cornwall Association of Tourist Attractions said the season had a "mixed start but a strong finish" with about half of its members in August reporting higher admissions and about seven in 10 reporting higher revenue than the year before.

In recent years long-running attractions including Flambards theme park in Helston , Dairyland near Newquay and Dingles Fairground Museum in Lifton have all closed.

Cornwall Visitor Alliance chairwoman Katie Warren said it had been a positive season for attractions.

"During the very hot days it was a bit quieter at the attractions but overall it did not affect them," she said.

"Visitor spend was slightly up - they were buying more at the restaurants and cafes. It was a much-needed boost for them because some attractions have suffered with rising costs."

Crealy director Josh Haywood credited "a really good summer" with a major £2m investment on two new family thrill rides.

He said the investment "certainly helped people through the doors" but the hotter weather also brought its own set of challenges including seats on rides being "too hot to sit in".

"It's always difficult when you're competing against the weather," he said.

"We have some world class beaches in the South West and it's very easy for people to go and have cheaper days out at the beach."

He said he was already making plans for next year on how to combat hot weather.

"Do we add more shaded areas? Do we add more water attractions?" he said.

Despite a strong start to summer, bosses at Canonteign Falls near Exeter said visitors started to tail off as hot weather persisted.

Chief executive Amy Greenman said it had been a "fantastic July" for the highest waterfall in the South West.

However, she said August was "slightly lower than expected" for visitors.

"Those heady heights we're used to in August were definitely not there," she said. "People were definitely feeling like a 220ft waterfall might be quite a lot in those really hot days."

Cornish heritage attraction Bodmin Jail reported a more widespread drop in visitors over the summer.

General manager Ashleigh Bettison said the jail was typically a "rainy day attraction" and this year it experienced a "huge decline" in numbers.

"When you only have two to three days of rain in a season, it's been really bad," she said.

Tourism bosses, however, said changing weather patterns were not as concerning as future economic uncertainty and investment in the sector.

They cited low confidence as a result of the cost of living, staff bills, uncertainty over higher fuel and a possible levy on tourism as major issues.

The government said "tourism is a major contributor to the South West economy"and "we are committed to supporting the sector".

"Our forthcoming Visitor Economy strategy will set out a long-term plan to help drive sustainable growth across the country," a spokesperson said.

"On top of that we are investing £3.38m to help destinations develop stronger visitor experiences and VisitBritain's £2m All on England's Coast campaign is encouraging people to book staycation breaks this autumn."

articles.title: New team heads to Antarctic port to save it from climate change
articles.summary: The mission aims to protect the base which is home to the world’s southernmost Post Office.
articles.body:
A new team of UK specialists is embarking on a 9,000-mile journey to Antarctica to protect a British science base threatened by climate change.

The UK Antarctic Heritage Trust (UKAHT), a Cambridge-based charity, is in its second year of a three-year mission to save Port Lockroy.

Its goal is to restore the site, which has the world's southernmost Post Office, museum, and more than 1,000 gentoo penguins.

This year's team will install beams and props to help the buildings withstand increased precipitation and snow loading, as well as monitor the penguins.

The site is more than 80 years old and faces structural deterioration due to rising temperatures and extreme weather on the rapidly warming Antarctic Peninsula.

After initial assessments revealed serious structural weaknesses, last year's team prepared the site ready for this season's interventions, which UKAHT said was the charity's "biggest ever conservation season" at Port Lockroy.

Port Lockroy faces escalating deterioration from age, climate change and environmental factors, said UKAHT.

A team of eight will spend five months at remote Base A, Port Lockroy on Goudier Island, while a field team of six specialists will travel further south to carry out the first comprehensive survey of another British heritage site, Wordie House , where one of the longest continuous climate records on the continent began.

The Port Lockroy team will be led by Carole McCullough, who previously worked in the RAF, and said: "I applied for the role looking for a bit of an adventure, and Antarctica is the ultimate adventure.

"The teamwork, the bonding, the appreciation of the place - it's all going to make for the most wonderful experience."

She will be joined by others with various life experiences including conservation carpenters and museum and mountain rescue specialists.

Camilla Nichol, UKAHT's chief executive officer, said: "With the demanding conservation season ahead at Port Lockroy and beyond to Wordie House, we have selected a team who bring specialist knowledge and understanding of the Antarctic environment, as well as some much needed enthusiasm and resilience.

"This is a huge year for us as we meet the growing challenges of climate change.

"Since Wordie House's records began in 1947, the Antarctic Peninsula has become one of the fastest-warming places on the planet and we see the impact every year on the wildlife and special places in our care."

articles.title: Republic of Ireland: Public sector strike begins
articles.summary: It comes amidst an an ongoing pay dispute between public sector workers and the Irish government.
articles.body:
More than 300,000 workers, including nurses, doctors, teachers and civil servants, are on strike across the Republic of Ireland.

It comes amid an ongoing pay dispute between public sector workers and the Irish government, with a further strike planned on 21 October.

It is expected schools could be closed with hospital appointments cancelled and picket lines formed across the country during the 24-hour strike.

At the end of September, more than 100,000 workers, including nurses, school staff and civil servants, moved to work-to-rule measures .

At the start of October, primary and secondary school teachers in the Republic began work-to-rule action .

Previously almost 97% of Fórsa members, who voted in an industrial ballot, did so in favour of action. It is the Republic's biggest public service union.

Brendan O'Brien divisional organiser of SIPTU, which represents public sector health and administration workers, previously said the "goodwill" of workers was a large part of what kept public services going.

However, he said the Irish government's failure to establish a basis for formal talks "left our members with no alternative but to act collectively".

On Tuesday Jack Chambers, the Republic's minister for expenditure, described the strike action as "deeply disappointing" saying it would cause significant disruption to the economy, with thousands of hospital appointments set to be cancelled and schools closed.

articles.title: 'Disgusting' car thefts ruin lives, say Essex victims
articles.summary: Thieves are adapting with technology, an expert says, as the county records one of the highest rates.
articles.body:
Victims of car thefts in Essex have told the BBC it is a crime that "ruins people's lives".

Home Office data showed Essex recorded the fourth highest rate of car theft per head of population in England and Wales between 2025-26, although its figures fell by more than 16% in the last year.

One victim said it was a "disgusting" crime, with another describing how their car had been stolen despite putting their keys in a signal-blocking pouch to deter thieves.

Essex Police said tackling vehicle crime was "a priority" for the force.

The Home Office data, compiled by the BBC, shows car theft data across England and Wales from 2015 to 2026.

In Essex, there were 4,646 car thefts between 2025-26 - up from 3,327 a decade ago - but lower than the 10-year peak of 5,979 thefts in 2023-24.

Across England and Wales, the percentage of recorded car theft offences resulting in a charge or summons has dropped from 10% in 2015-16 to 3% in 2025-26.

Claire Cornell, a children support worker from Clacton-on-Sea, needed her Ford Kuga for work - but woke up on 2 September to find it had been stolen in the early hours.

"At first I thought maybe I'd mis-parked it somewhere," she said, adding she had kept her keys in a Faraday pouch which blocks their signal, but thieves had used other tactics to get into her car.

"I literally rang [Essex Police], and they were like, 'okay, we'll just log it'. And that was it - they weren't helpful at all," she said.

Essex Police said an officer had spoken "at length with [Claire] about the incident, her concerns and the impact the theft had had on her", and the force had updated her on the investigation and offered "safeguarding, reassurance and crime prevention advice", as well as reviewing relevant CCTV footage and making door-to-door enquiries.

Another victim, who did not wish to be named, said car theft was a "disgusting" crime.

The woman, who works as a professional cleaner in south Essex, said thieves stole her vehicle which contained all her cleaning materials.

She said she quickly bought another car as she needed it for work, only for her original vehicle to be found just days later.

"I lost about £1,000 [selling the replacement car], and then on top of that… my insurance went up by £60 a month, which is a lot," she said.

Other victims told how their security camera or doorbell had failed to record the thieves in action, as they had used a wifi blocker to kill the signal.

Nick Gover, from Thurrock, who runs car security firm Auto Communications, said thieves were constantly adapting their techniques.

"You'd see the thieves scanning the house for the car keys, so then people were putting their keys in the Faraday boxes, which still work if they try to steal the car that way," he said.

"[Now] they're also finding ways to plug into the car without actually accessing the inside of the car first."

Gover said as well as signal-blocking pouches, immobilisers and steering locks would slow thieves down, but advancements in car technology were helping thieves as well.

"Whatever makes things easier for the user makes it easier for the thieves," he said.

A spokesperson for Essex Police said: "We understand the impact having a vehicle stolen can have", adding that the force had a "coordinated, intelligence-led approach focused on preventing offences, recovering stolen vehicles, disrupting those responsible and bringing offenders to justice".

Essex Police said its crime figures, covering the 12 months to August 2026, "show vehicle theft fell by 9% across the county, with 470 fewer offences recorded than in the previous 12 months".

The spokesperson added that "when compared with the 12 months to August 2023, we have more than doubled the number of vehicle theft investigations solved".

"Anyone who discovers their vehicle has been stolen should report it to us as soon as possible. If a theft is happening right now or a crime is in progress, always call 999," they said.

Further theft prevention advice can be found on Essex Police's website .

articles.title: Norfolk amputee asked for more proof for blue badge renewal
articles.summary: Nigel Ward, 71, says he believes fraudulent claims have led to more scrutiny of genuine applicants.
articles.body:
For amputee Nigel Ward, the evidence is undeniable.

The 71-year-old from King's Lynn assumed that providing photos showing his missing leg would be enough proof to get his blue badge renewed by Norfolk County Council.

But Ward has been asked to verify his disability further, with one council worker suggesting amputees can run marathons - a level of physical endurance he insists he does not have.

Norfolk County Council has insisted it is following correct procedures. But Ward, who lost his leg following a medical incident on a cruise three years ago, has been left "very disheartened" and says he worries it will affect his independence.

He added: "I am a genuine applicant, not a benefits cheat and I need a blue badge."

Norfolk County Council said there was no renewal process and that applicants had to provide evidence with each application, to prove ongoing eligibility.

The process still applies to those who have a permanent disability.

A spokesperson said: "We know how important blue badges are for helping people to remain independent.

"We have to work within the guidance set for us by the Department for Transport, which includes detailed guidance how eligibility should be assessed through evidence and assessments.

"Applicants must adequately evidence the difficulties they experience whilst walking, this applies to those reapplying for an expiring blue badge as well as first time applications."

They said evidence could include letters, reports or details of treatment from a medical professional.

Ward said he could not provide medical evidence of limited mobility, as he no longer needed to attend consultations or meetings with doctors after receiving his prosthetic limb.

"I am regarded as independent now," he said, "and would only need their assistance if something went wrong, either with the prosthetic limb or the stump."

Ward, who lives with his wife Gill, first applied successfully for a blue badge three years ago and said the process had been relatively simple before.

Without the permit, journeys will become "troublesome to say the least", he says, and he has not been told what specific evidence to provide to complete his application.

After his plight was raised on social media by his daughter, Ward said several people had been in touch to say they faced similar issues getting blue badges renewed.

He said he believed fraudulent claims had led to more scrutiny of genuine applicants.

Disabled Motoring UK and Equal Lives, two Norfolk-based disability charities, previously warned blue badge users frequently face abuse and suspicion from other drivers when parking in disabled bays.

articles.title: Rare artworks at Norwich display help tell Bayeux Tapestry story
articles.summary: They include a silver-gilt reliquary similar to those seen in the Bayeux Tapestry, say organisers.
articles.body:
A collection of special objects with connections to scenes in the Bayeux Tapestry is to go on display - aptly in a Norman castle.

Twenty-one items - including a rare silver-gilt reliquary box - have been loaned to Norwich Castle Museum by the Wyvern Collection in London, some of them for the very first time.

"In the Bayeux Tapestry, you see King Harold swearing an oath on reliquaries and we've got a reliquary that is actually from the period," said curator Tim Pestell.

The aim is to "give a sense of how rich and complex the world in which they were made for was", said Dr Susannah Kingwill, director of the Wyvern Research Institute.

Kingwill said the display was "capitalising on the moment of interest that's being garnered by the display of the Bayeux Tapestry at the British Museum" and offered "a very rich picture of the material culture that was in existence in the period of the Norman Conquest".

The exhibition is part of a series of events around Britain to mark the arrival of the Bayeux Tapestry in England.

It tells the story of the Norman Conquest and one of its key moments is when the Anglo-Saxon Harold is supposed to have sworn an oath to help William, Duke of Normandy take the English throne.

To make the oath binding, he is shown placing his hands on two reliquaries - beautifully crafted boxes which would have contained relics of saints.

Instead, Harold claimed the throne, setting the scene for William's invasion.

Five key scenes from the Bayeux Tapestry, and the story they tell

The Norman Conquest transformed England by introducing a new king, a new language, and new forms of art and architecture.

Curator of archaeology Pestell added: "Anglo-Saxon England effectively looks to the northern world; it's an Anglo-Scandinavian population, especially so in East Anglia.

"But after the Norman Conquest, England looks to France and it becomes part of that Norman world, where a whole different artistic repertoire is being used."

An example of this is a 12th Century wooden sculpture of the Virgin Mary.

"The proportions are completely different [from Saxon designs]; they're really long, thin, stretched out figures," he said.

Pestell likened the way it gesticulates with its hands to the story-telling revealed in the tapestry.

He said: "Every scene is linked by people gesturing with their hands, with their faces."

The Wyvern Collection holds about 3,000 objects, but is particularly well known for its collection of sculptures, metalwork objects and ivories from the medieval period.

However, medieval metalwork is less likely to have survived down the centuries, because it could be melted down for reuse, said Kingwill.

So, one of her highlights from the exhibition is a bronze candlestick of a kneeling young man.

She said: "It measures around 13.5cm (5.3in) high and it's just a really extraordinarily beautiful object for something that maybe seems almost commonplace.

"I think it shows the technical skill and ingenuity of the people that were making these items as well."

Other unusual exhibits include the earliest known standing sculpture of the Virgin and Child, made at about the same time as the Battle of Hastings - and a magnificently carved ivory hunting horn.

Another highlight is the Norwich Friends' Tapestry, a 19 metre-long (62ft) embroidery telling the story of two East of England rebellions against William the Conqueror.

Visitors will be able to view rarely seen 19th Century hand-painted plaster cast details from the Bayeux Tapestry from 12 November to 10 January.

The exhibition forms part of the preparations for the European Year of the Normans next year, marking 1,000 years since the birth of William the Conqueror.

It has been supported by the Norwich Freemen's Charity and the British Museum.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia overturns death sentence for man over Facebook comment, Sri Lanka says
articles.summary: Anojan Sivarasa's case sent shockwaves through Sri Lanka, spurring diplomatic efforts to seek clemency.
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia's Supreme Court has set aside the death sentence handed to a Sri Lankan migrant worker over a comment he made on Facebook, Colombo's Deputy Foreign Minister Arun Hemachandra said.

Anojan Sivarasa, 27, was sentenced to death in September after a Saudi appellate court convicted him of blasphemy against Islam and the Prophet Muhammad over his comment.

The case sent shockwaves through Sri Lanka , spurring diplomatic efforts to seek clemency.

Saudi Arabia's top court set aside the sentence on Wednesday, Hemachandra said in a post on Facebook, where he thanked the authorities and legal teams of both nations for their efforts.

In late June, footage of a young Muslim man kicking a dog following Hindu pilgrims circulated widely on social media, triggering religious arguments online.

During the exchange, a user posted derogatory remarks about a Hindu deity, leading Sivarasa to respond in Tamil insulting the Prophet Muhammad.

Although Sivarasa promptly deleted the comment and posted an apology video, a screenshot of it was brought to the attention of his employer and Saudi officials, leading to his arrest in July.

It is not clear if there will be further legal proceedings or whether Sivarasa will remain in detention, and for how long. He was initially sentenced to five years in prison as well as a fine of three million Saudi riyals ($0.8m; £0.6m) by the Al-Ahsa Criminal Court.

Faizer Mustafa, a Sri Lankan lawmaker who is involved in legal negotiations with Saudi Arabia regarding Sivarasa's case, confirmed to BBC Sinhala that Saudi Arabia had overturned the death sentence, adding that they are reviewing the Supreme Court's latest ruling.

Sivarasa's family had earlier said they have had no direct contact with him since 28 September.

International rights groups had also joined calls for Saudi to spare his life.

"Saudi authorities should end their use of abusive laws to hand out extraordinary sentences for speech-related offenses, especially against migrant workers who are already in a vulnerable position with limited protections," Joey Shea, senior Saudi Arabia researcher at Human Rights Watch, said on Tuesday.

articles.title: Turkey police raid opposition TV, halting live broadcasts
articles.summary: Halk TV says its staff are unable to enter the building in Istanbul and a new manager has been appointed.
articles.body:
Turkish police have raided the headquarters of a pro-opposition TV channel, halting its live broadcasts.

Halk TV said its employees were unable to enter the building in Istanbul on Wednesday morning, and that a new manager had been appointed to run the channel.

Reports in Turkish media said financial crimes police were searching the building and 17 arrest warrants had been issued in the raid linked to the channel's owner.

Halk TV has been seen by many in the country as being close to the opposition Republican People's Party (CHP). It often voices criticism of President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan's ruling AK party.

In May, a Turkish court removed the CHP leadership from running the party , in a move the opposition said further cemented Erdoğan's grip on power.

Meanwhile, Istanbul's popular Mayor Ekrem Imamoğlu, widely seen as Erdoğan's biggest political rival, has been in prison for over a year over corruption accusations. He denies all the charges.

articles.title: Photos: Student protest in Albania prompts violent clashes with police
articles.summary: Protesters in Tirana throw bricks at the Education Ministry building as police respond with tear gas and water cannon.
articles.body:
Student protests over education and social inequality in Albania turned violent as police clashed with demonstrators in the capital, Tirana.

On Tuesday, hundreds of students hurled bricks and concrete blocks at the Education Ministry building, prompting security forces to respond with tear gas and water cannon. Police detained several protesters as the confrontation spilled into nearby streets.

Student organisers said the nationwide protest was driven by deteriorating conditions at universities, high education costs, limited financial support and bleak employment prospects after graduation. Some also voiced anger at widening inequality and a political system they see as failing young people.

“What Albania needs is a revolution, a change, a complete overthrow of the system because it can’t go on like this,” protester Luljeta Kola said, describing “deep social injustice” and a growing gulf between rich and poor.

Deputy Prime Minister Albana Kociu condemned the unrest, writing on Facebook that “violence has not been, is not, and will never be a solution”.

The demonstration comes amid a broader wave of student activism across Europe, including weeks of high school protests and blockades in France.

articles.title: ‘Massive’ Russian attack on Ukraine kills at least six, cuts power in Kyiv
articles.summary: At least six people have been killed in overnight Russian attacks across Ukraine.
articles.body:
Russian air attacks have killed at least six people in Ukraine and caused power cuts in parts of the capital Kyiv, days after United States President Donald Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” in the more-than four year war.

The ⁠Russian Defence Ministry said on Wednesday that its forces had carried out a “massive” strike ‌against communications and energy infrastructure facilities ⁠in Ukraine, the Interfax ⁠news ⁠agency reported.

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko urged people to remain in shelters.

“Energy facilities in Kyiv and the surrounding region have come under a massive ballistic missile strike. There are power disruptions in the capital,” he wrote on Telegram.

DTEK, Ukraine’s largest private energy provider, said the attack had caused emergency power cuts in several urban districts of Kyiv.

A Russian strike on a multistorey building in the capital’s Desnianskyi district killed two people, while another attack in Golosiivsky district killed one, Ukraine’s state emergency service said.

The Ukrainian military also reported that two people were killed and six wounded in Russian attacks on the Dnipropetrovsk region. Another person was killed in the southeastern Zaporizhzhia region.

Further Russian missile attacks were reported in the Kharkiv and Zhytomyr regions, while other strikes hit Sumy and Chernigiv.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russian attacks on Kyiv had come without Ukraine receiving advance warning from its Western allies.

“A Russian ballistic missile attack on Kyiv. Once again, no early warning from our partners,” he wrote on Facebook. “This is absolutely unjust: when they are destroying our infrastructure, and Ukraine is not even receiving early warnings about ballistic missile launches.”

The president said Ukraine detected the missiles only as they neared Kyiv.

He also accused Russia of violating the “energy ceasefire” Trump announced on Sunday.

“A targeted Russian ballistic missile strike specifically against energy infrastructure – the very infrastructure covered by the ceasefire announced by the American President,” he wrote on X.

“The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale – Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States.”

Russia also reported Ukrainian drone strikes overnight. The governor of Russia’s Saratov region, Roman Busargin, said a Ukrainian drone strike had killed one person in the city of Balakovo.

Busargin said all ⁠infrastructure ⁠facilities were operating as usual. Balakovo is home ⁠to a data centre of Russia’s ⁠top lender Sberbank, a ⁠nuclear power ⁠plant and a hydropower station, whose dam spans ‌the Volga River, among other facilities.

Moscow mayor Sergey Sobyanin said air defence forces had downed nearly 500 drones flying towards the Russian capital overnight. Russian authorities said about 160 more were brought down over the Rostov region, while others targeted Moscow.

Russia’s military later put the number of downed Ukrainian drones overnight at 902, of which 180 were shot down near the capital Moscow.

articles.title: Swimmer Archie Goodburn to meet prime minister over cancer funding
articles.summary: The Scottish athlete, who has inoperable brain tumours, previously made a tearful plea for more investment in brain cancer research on BBC Breakfast.
articles.body:
Swimmer Archie Goodburn is to meet the prime minister later after making a tearful plea for more investment to be put into brain cancer research.

The Scottish athlete, who was diagnosed with three inoperable brain tumours two years ago, said the Downing Street meeting offered a "unique opportunity for change".

He previously called for Andy Burnham to introduce a brain cancer lead to give patients a chance to "fight for their lives" during an appearance on BBC Breakfast.

Goodburn, 25, cried while looking down the camera, saying he was "on my knees begging" for help to ease the "unbearable suffering" of patients and their families.

Burnham later contacted Goodburn on social media to set up the meeting at Downing Street.

Goodburn reached the final of the 50m breaststroke at the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

He said he went for medical tests after suffering from numbness and seizures during training for the 2024 Olympic trials.

He was diagnosed with three large oligodendrogliomas , a rare type of cancer which can affect the brain and spinal cord.

The Edinburgh-born swimmer underwent chemotherapy and radiotherapy to treat the tumours, but surgery to remove them was found to be impossible.

Burnham invites swimmer Goodburn to meeting after cancer funding plea

Swimmer Goodburn diagnosed with inoperable brain tumours

During his appearance on BBC Breakfast, Goodburn called for more resource to be put into research and care, and for clinical trials happening elsewhere to be brought to the UK.

"Please establish a national brain cancer lead and give us a chance to fight for our lives because the things that patients are going through out there are unbelievable and so unjust," he said.

"There are clinical trials around the world, in the US, in Australia, in China, that could change lives. We are not seeing them in the UK and it is unfair and unjust.

"Please invest and make the difference. I'm on my knees begging for - not just my own life - but for those of my best friends and those that are affected and the families around the country."

Goodburn added: "This has to change. It's been going for too long and the suffering is unbearable."

Ahead of the meeting, Goodburn said he hoped it would be a "unique opportunity for change."

"We cannot accept the status quo in the system, we cannot be risk-averse. People are dying," he said.

"My advocacy has opened doors to have conversations at the highest level of government about the injustices faced by the brain tumour community and campaign for change for myself and for them.

"But I hope I can also inspire people on an individual level."

Charity Brain Tumour Research said the disease was the cancer most likely to kill patients under 40 in the UK.

They said charities made up more than 75% of the total national investment in brain tumour research, with the government funding sitting at 25%.

The Rare Cancers Bill, led by Edinburgh South West MP Scott Arthur, became law earlier this year.

The legislation aims to incentivise research and investment into the treatment of rare types of cancer, defined as those affecting fewer than 1 in every 2,000 people.

Goodburn said that did not go far enough and a dedicated brain cancer lead would allow for greater focus on specific research and trials.

Arthur said the act was "vital" to driving research needed into the condition, but that Goodburn's meeting with Burnham could lead to further work in the field.

"There is real opportunity in the sector to dismantle the barriers to research that charities, clinicians, and researchers have known about for decades," he said.

"Having met Archie a number of times I know he is a fantastic advocate for the brain tumour community.

"I hope his meeting with the prime minister is a moment for concrete progress to be made."
